question: A ticketing startup runs its public API on Cloud Run. A new revision changes the pricing logic, and the team wants to expose it to only 5% of production traffic, watch error rates for an hour, and then gradually increase the share. They want to use native Cloud Run capabilities. What should you do?
options: Deploy the new revision as a separate Cloud Run service and configure Cloud DNS weighted records to send 5% of requests to it
Deploy the new revision normally so that it receives 100% of traffic, and immediately roll back if errors appear
Deploy the new revision with the --no-traffic flag, then use traffic splitting (gcloud run services update-traffic) to send 5% of requests to the new revision and increase the percentage over time
Create a second Cloud Run region and deploy the new revision there so that only users routed to that region see it
explanation: Cloud Run supports deploying a revision without routing traffic to it and then splitting traffic between revisions by percentage, which is the native way to run a canary and to progressively migrate traffic while watching metrics. DNS weighting across separate services (option A) is imprecise because of client caching and requires duplicating the service. Deploying to 100% (option B) exposes all users to the risk that a canary is meant to avoid. A new region (option D) changes latency for users and does not give a controlled percentage.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run canary releases): Cloud Run supports deploying a revision without routing traffic to it and then splitting traffic between revisions by percentage, which is the native way to run a canary and to progressively migrate traffic while watching metrics.

question: A hospital's patient-portal backend runs on a managed instance group behind an external Application Load Balancer. The application's session-handling code is not compatible between versions, so the two versions must never serve traffic at the same time, and the operations team must be able to revert to the previous version within one minute if problems appear. Which deployment strategy should you use?
options: Blue/green: deploy the new version to a second managed instance group, verify it, switch the load balancer backend service to the new group in one step, and keep the old group running until the release is confirmed so that switching back is instant
Rolling update on the existing managed instance group with maxSurge set to 100% so that all instances are replaced quickly
Canary update on the existing managed instance group, running the new template on 10% of instances for an hour before completing the rollout
In-place update by SSH-ing into each instance and restarting the application with the new binary during a maintenance window
explanation: Blue/green deployment switches all traffic between two complete environments at once, so old and new versions never serve concurrently, and rollback is simply pointing the backend back at the previous group, which meets the one-minute requirement. Rolling and canary updates (options B and C) both intentionally run mixed versions during the rollout, violating the compatibility constraint. In-place manual updates (option D) are slow, error-prone toil with no fast rollback.

question: A payment gateway runs on a regional managed instance group of 20 VMs that is sized exactly for peak load. The team wants to roll out a new instance template automatically without ever reducing serving capacity below 20 healthy instances and without manual intervention. How should you configure the update?
options: Use an opportunistic update so that instances are replaced only when the autoscaler happens to recreate them

Replacing all 20 at once (option B) creates a full outage. maxUnavailable of 5 (option C) explicitly allows capacity to drop to 15, violating the requirement.

question: A media company's GKE Standard cluster hosts a stateful video-encoding service that needs up to 90 seconds to finish in-flight work before a pod can be safely terminated. Spot VMs (option E) can be preempted at any time, which is worse for stateful, long-running work.

question: A streaming music company wants developers to merge and deploy code to production several times a day, but the product team wants new user-facing features to be shown first to employees, then to 1% of users, and turned off instantly if something goes wrong, all without another deployment. question: A logistics company needs to rename the column customer_ref to customer_id in a heavily used Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL table. The service that uses the table runs on GKE with rolling deployments, so old and new pods coexist for several minutes, and the business requires zero downtime. Which two practices should you follow? question: A government agency's QA team must test every new revision of a Cloud Run service against the production configuration and data sources before any citizen traffic reaches it. question: An online retailer uses Cloud Deploy to promote releases to production. question: A ride-sharing company's trip-pricing service on GKE Autopilot returns a burst of HTTP 502 and connection-reset errors for a few seconds every time a new version is rolled out or a node is upgraded, even though readiness probes are configured. Investigation shows that pods are terminated while the load balancer is still sending them requests. What should you do to make rollouts and upgrades invisible to users?
options: Increase the number of replicas so that the proportion of failed requests during each rollout is smaller
Switch from a rolling update to a Recreate strategy so that all pods are replaced at once during a short window

Add a preStop hook that delays shutdown for a few seconds so that endpoint removal propagates before the process stops, handle SIGTERM in the application to drain in-flight requests, and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds long enough for the drain to complete
explanation: The errors come from a race between pod termination and endpoint deregistration: the load balancer briefly continues to route to a pod that has already started shutting down. A preStop sleep gives the endpoint controller and load balancer time to remove the pod, proper SIGTERM handling lets in-flight requests finish, and a sufficient termination grace period ensures Kubernetes does not kill the process prematurely; together they make rollouts and node upgrades zero-error events. More replicas (option A) only dilutes the errors. Recreate (option B) causes a full outage on every deploy. Removing readiness probes (option C) addresses startup, not shutdown, and would route traffic to pods that are not yet ready.

question: A global gaming company serves players from Cloud Run services deployed in six regions behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Every release currently goes to all six regions simultaneously through a script, and a recent bad release caused a worldwide outage for twelve minutes. The company wants to limit the blast radius of releases while keeping the process automated. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Continue deploying to all regions at once but shorten the deployment script so that a rollback can be executed faster
Deploy new releases to a single region only and route all global traffic there during the release to simplify observation

Model the six regions as sequential targets in a Cloud Deploy pipeline, starting with the lowest-traffic region, with a bake period and automated SLI verification between stages, so that a bad release is detected and stopped before it reaches the remaining regions
Deploy only on weekends when player counts are lowest so that an outage affects fewer users
explanation: Rolling a release out region by region, beginning with the smallest population and waiting for verified health before proceeding, is the standard way to bound blast radius in multi-region systems; Cloud Deploy supports sequential targets with verification and automated promotion, keeping the process fully automated. Faster rollback of a global deployment (option A) still exposes all users to the initial failure. Concentrating all global traffic in one region (option B) creates a massive capacity and latency risk. Weekend-only releases (option D) reduce exposure only marginally and slow delivery without addressing blast radius.
hint: Core Rule (Regional progressive rollout): Rolling a release out region by region, beginning with the smallest population and waiting for verified health before proceeding, is the standard way to bound blast radius in multi-region systems; Cloud Deploy supports sequential targets with verification and automated promotion, keeping the process fully automated.

question: A healthcare SaaS provider has a policy that any production release must be revertible within five minutes. A recent attempt to roll back a GKE service failed because the previous container image had been deleted from the registry and the new release had already altered the database schema in an incompatible way. Which two practices should you adopt to make the five-minute rollback objective achievable? (Choose two.)
options: Retain previously deployed images in Artifact Registry, reference images by immutable digest in manifests, and configure cleanup policies so that images currently or recently in production are never purged
Store container images only on developer laptops so that they can be pushed quickly during a rollback
Apply schema changes in the same transaction as the application deployment so that both can be reverted together
Grant every developer cluster-admin on the production cluster so that anyone can execute a rollback
Make every database schema change backward compatible with the previous application version, so that rolling back the application never requires a schema rollback
explanation: Fast rollback depends on two things: the previous artifact must still exist and be exactly identifiable (immutable digests and retention-aware cleanup policies in Artifact Registry), and the database must still work with the previous code, which is guaranteed by making schema changes backward compatible rather than coupling them to the release. Images on laptops (option B) are unreliable and unauditable. Coupling schema and application changes (option C) makes rollbacks slower and riskier, not faster, because schema changes are often irreversible. Broad cluster-admin grants (option D) violate least privilege and do not address the technical causes of the failed rollback.

question: A mid-sized retailer has a small operations team with limited Kubernetes expertise. question: An ad-tech company's on-call engineers are paged about once a night because a legacy reporting process on a Compute Engine VM leaks memory until it must be restarted; the documented runbook consists of a single command that restarts the service. question: A travel company runs a stateless booking API on a regional managed instance group of 30 VMs. It wants to validate a new instance template on a small subset of real production traffic for a day before rolling it out to the whole group, and it wants the MIG to keep managing autoscaling and autohealing during that period. explanation: Cloud Deploy's approval feature blocks a rollout to an approval-required target until a principal with the Approver role acts, and its role model separates who can create and promote releases from who can approve them; combined with per-target execution service accounts, developers never need write access to the production cluster, and Cloud Deploy plus Cloud Audit Logs record who released, approved, and deployed. An email convention (option A) is not an enforceable control. Manual kubectl by the release manager (option C) removes automation and creates its own audit and consistency problems. A Slack emoji gate (option D) is custom, weakly authenticated, and not a recognized approval record.

whyWrong.0: Option A ("Give developers the Cloud Deploy Operator role on all targets, and ask them to email the release manager before promoting to production") is incorrect because it does not meet the scenario's core requirement; Option B (Mark the production target as requiring approval, grant deve) is the Google Cloud recommended pattern here.
